clue.text: Wise guy hurt, plonker initially poking nasty wound

parts.note: to smart is to sting or hurt

indicators.note: something poking into another thing pushes inside it, so one piece goes within the other
wound is the past of wind, as in twisted round, so the letters are coiled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

parts.note: opening letter of plonker

explanation.surface: A know-all gets hurt when some idiot jabs at a horrible injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound' looks like a noun, the injury, but it is the verb wind in the past tense. A plonker is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A smartypants is a mocking name for someone who shows off their cleverness, the same sarcastic sense as calling a person a wise guy.

clue.text: Football club, northern champions at the top in richest team formed ultimate in plutocracy?

indicators.note: formed means shaped or made up, so these letters are fashioned into a new arrangement

parts.note: N is the standard abbreviation for northern

indicators.note: in a down entry the top of a word is its beginning, so its first letter is taken

parts.note: first letter of champions
taken as written, as anagram material

indicators.note: ultimate means final, so the very last letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: last letter of plutocracy

explanation.surface: A wealthy northern football side, title winners, built from money: a club of plutocrats.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is barbed: the club was bought by very rich owners and became champions, so 'richest team' and 'plutocracy' describe it while also supplying letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Manchester City is a Premier League side based in the north of England, an example of a professional soccer team.

clue.text: Lippy daughter seen in French street

indicators.note: something seen in a place is inside it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: rue is French for street
D is the usual abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A cheeky girl is spotted out on a road in France.
explanation.walkthrough: Lippy is British slang for cheeky, giving lip or back-talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lippy answers back insolently, which is being impolite or disrespectful in speech.

clue.text: Eager boy finally in paid work

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: earning is getting paid for work

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of the word is used

parts.note: last letter of boy

explanation.surface: A keen lad is at last taking on a paying job.
explanation.walkthrough: The kept letter goes in at the front edge of the other piece, which still counts as being in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A yearning look is a longing, wishful one, so the adjective carries the sense of keenly wanting something.

clue.text: A wild horse on the beach

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so these letters run free into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: An untamed pony gallops across the sand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild horse' reads as one picture, but the adjective is the signal acting on the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To be ashore is to be on land at the water's edge rather than at sea, the place a beach occupies.

clue.text: Exclamation of disapproval about a job

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: tsk is the clicking sound of disapproval
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tuts at the thought of a piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like 'concerning', but it means around.
explanation.definitionFit: A task is a piece of work to be done, a plain synonym for an assignment or chore.

clue.text: Politically unstable country needing a hand?

definitions.text: Politically unstable country needing a hand?

parts.note: surface reading: a shaky state that needs outside help
setter's reading: a hand is a bunch of a certain yellow fruit

explanation.walkthrough: 'Needing a hand' sounds like asking for help; a hand is also the cluster in which bananas grow and are sold.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a small, corrupt state dependent on one export crop and run by an unstable government.

clue.text: Common, 120 for a dollar it seems?

definitions.text: Common, 120 for a dollar it seems?

parts.note: straight reading: plentiful and cheap
setter's reading: a dollar is ten ten-cent coins, so 120 items for it means twelve per coin

explanation.walkthrough: Do the arithmetic: a dollar is ten US ten-cent coins, so 120 for a dollar works out at twelve per coin, the literal price in the idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The American idiom describes something so plentiful that it is worth little, a fair match for ordinary or commonplace.

clue.text: Play one of those perfect union men

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a comedy by Oscar Wilde

definitions.text: one of those perfect union men
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a flawless partner in marriage, the union

explanation.walkthrough: 'Union men' suggests trade unionists, but the union is marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde's 1895 comedy carries this title, and literally the phrase describes a model spouse who is male.

clue.text: Toy in pile at worst malfunctioning

indicators.note: something malfunctioning is not working properly, so the letters fall out of order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A plaything sits in a heap, broken at its very worst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pile at worst' reads as nonsense on the surface, a hint that the words are raw material.
explanation.definitionFit: A water pistol is a children's plaything that squirts a jet of water, a specific example of a toy.

clue.text: Long, first of holes in one

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: a hole in one in golf is called an ace

indicators.note: first of means the opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: opening letter of holes

explanation.surface: A long golf hole, and someone hits a hole in one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long' looks like an adjective about the hole, but it is the verb to long, and 'one' stands for a hole in one, an ace.
explanation.definitionFit: To ache for something is to yearn or pine for it, the same verb sense as to long for it.

clue.text: Opening bars in Spain troublesome

indicators.note: in shows the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: Bars that open in Spain are causing trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening bars' suggests pubs or bars opening their doors; here they are the first bars of a piece of music.
explanation.definitionFit: An intro is the short introduction of a song or piece, its first few measures before the main part.

clue.text: Cordial evidently unrefrigerated?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: not chilled, of a drink

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cordial' looks like the fruit drink, which you might keep in a fridge; it is the adjective meaning friendly.
explanation.definitionFit: A warm greeting is a friendly, hearty one, and something not kept in a fridge is literally not cold.

clue.text: Try joke

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an attempt, as in have a go
second meaning: a wisecrack or quip

explanation.walkthrough: Both words are nouns here: have a crack at it, and make a crack about someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally a crack is an attempt at something and also a witty or cutting remark.

clue.text: Bent, also breaking through

indicators.note: breaking into something means forcing a way inside it, so one piece enters the other

parts.note: by can mean through or by way of
and means also, in addition

explanation.surface: Something crooked is also bursting its way through.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Through' looks like part of 'breaking through', but it is the outer piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Bandy legs curve outward at the knee, so the word describes limbs that are bowed or curved.

clue.text: Reformed sinner, he is put in sacred place

indicators.note: reformed means made over into a new shape, so the letters are rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material
taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A sinner who has mended his ways is placed in a holy spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformed sinner' is a stock phrase, so the signal hides inside a familiar pairing.
explanation.definitionFit: To enshrine is literally to place a relic or image in a shrine, a holy place set aside for it.

clue.text: Country where Tibetan priest, losing head, follows God

indicators.note: losing its head means the front letter is removed
follows sets the order, putting one piece after the other

parts.note: Pan is the Greek god of the wild
a lama is a Tibetan Buddhist monk, minus its first letter

explanation.surface: A land where a beheaded Tibetan monk comes after a deity.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists the priest first, but 'follows' puts the god in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Panama is a nation in Central America, known for its canal, so it is an example of a country.

clue.text: Game over in league, stuffing knocked out

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another
with the stuffing knocked out only the outside is left, so just the end letters stay

parts.note: league with its middle letters removed leaves only the first and last
over can mean across, as in a bridge over the river

explanation.surface: A match is over in the league, the team having been thrashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game over' reads as one phrase, but 'Game' is the definition and 'over' the inner piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacrosse is a team sport played with netted sticks and a ball, so it is an example of a game.

clue.text: Run through beginning of recitative in musical work

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: a piece is a musical composition

indicators.note: beginning of means the opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: opening letter of recitative

explanation.surface: Someone rehearses the start of a sung passage in a musical composition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run through' looks like rehearse, which fits the music; it means stab. Recitative is the speech-like singing between arias in opera.
explanation.definitionFit: To run someone through with a sword is to stab right into them, the same act as to penetrate or puncture.

clue.text: Diagnose rash in US city

indicators.note: rash means reckless or hasty, so the letters tumble into a careless new order

parts.note: taken as written, as anagram material

explanation.surface: A doctor identifies a skin rash in an American town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' wants to be the skin complaint being diagnosed; it is the adjective meaning hasty.
explanation.definitionFit: San Diego is a large Californian city near the Mexican border, an example of a city in the United States.

clue.text: Food served with bangers that is for old club

parts.note: bangers are sausages, traditionally served with mashed potato
i.e. is the abbreviation for that is

explanation.surface: The side dish that goes with sausages is fit for an old-fashioned gentlemen's club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' suggests a members' club with old-fashioned food; it is a golf club. Bangers and mash is a classic British dish of sausages and mashed potato.
explanation.definitionFit: A mashie was an iron golf club of earlier times, roughly matching a modern five iron, so it is an obsolete club.

clue.text: Fire pocket

definitions.meaning: first meaning: dismiss from a job
second meaning: a pouch or bag

explanation.walkthrough: Both look like ordinary nouns or verbs about flames and clothing; each is one meaning of the same short word.
explanation.definitionFit: To sack an employee is to dismiss them, and a sack is also a bag or pouch for holding things.

clue.text: Frightening, as armpits may be?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: scary or dangerous, informally

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the second part is a playful example rather than a dictionary definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally a hairy moment is a scary, risky one, while literally the word means covered with hair.

clue.text: Squeeze toe on massive giant

indicators.note: on means added after, so one piece is placed next to the other

parts.note: to hug is to squeeze in an embrace

indicators.note: the toe is at the foot, so only the bottom or final letter of the word is kept

parts.note: final letter of massive

explanation.surface: Someone crushes the foot of an enormous ogre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Massive' sits next to 'giant' as if both describe the ogre, but 'massive' only donates its foot letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Giant used as an adjective means enormous, a straightforward synonym for very large.

clue.text: A croft briefly seen in the distance

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
a croft is a small farm in Scotland, cut short

explanation.surface: A small farmstead glimpsed far off.
explanation.walkthrough: A croft is a small rented farm in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Afar means at or from a great way off, as in seen from afar, matching a remote position.

clue.text: Bread bundle

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a wad or bundle of banknotes wound up together

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' tempts toward money slang alongside 'bundle'; each word is a separate meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll is a small individual loaf, and also a cylindrical wad of something such as banknotes or cloth.

clue.text: Wonderful to be far from our home?

definitions.text: to be far from our home?
definitions.meaning: second meaning: literally off planet Earth

explanation.walkthrough: 'Our home' is the Earth, and the question mark flags reading the idiom literally.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom praises something as extraordinarily good, while taken literally it places you beyond the planet.

clue.text: Easy job coming to stop in building unit

parts.note: a breeze is something done with no effort
to block is to stop or obstruct

explanation.surface: A cushy job comes to a halt on a building site.
explanation.walkthrough: A breeze block is the British name for a cinder block, a light concrete brick.
explanation.definitionFit: These lightweight concrete bricks are a standard component in walls, so each is a construction module.
